at vaske.explanation: "At vaske" means "to wash", for clothes, dishes, your hands or the car: "Jeg vasker tøj" (I wash clothes). To wash yourself, say "vaske sig" (to wash oneself). "At vaske op" means "to do the dishes".

sentence.da: Jeg vil **vaske** tøjet, for det er snavset.
sentence.en: I want to wash the clothes, because they are dirty.

at vaske op.explanation: "At vaske op" means "to do the dishes" by hand. The little word "op" (up) stays after the verb: "Jeg vasker op" (I do the dishes). Do not mix it up with "at vaske" (to wash), which is used for clothes, hands or the car.

sentence.da: Efter maden skal jeg **vaske op**, så tallerkenerne bliver rene.
sentence.en: After the meal I have to do the dishes so the plates get clean.

at vaske sig.explanation: "At vaske sig" means "to wash yourself". The little word "sig" (oneself) becomes "mig" (myself) when you talk about yourself: "jeg vasker mig". If you wash something else, you drop it: "at vaske hænder" (to wash hands) or "at vaske tøj" (to wash clothes).

sentence.da: Han er snavset, så han skal **vaske sig**.
sentence.en: He is dirty, so he has to wash himself.

at veje.explanation: "At veje" means "to weigh". You can weigh something ("Jeg vejer pakken", I weigh the package) or have a certain weight ("Jeg vejer 70 kilo", I weigh 70 kilos).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **veje** pakken, så jeg kan se, hvor tung den er.
sentence.en: I want to weigh the package so I can see how heavy it is.

at vente.explanation: "At vente" means "to wait": "Jeg venter på bussen" (I am waiting for the bus). You wait for something with "vente på" (wait for). A useful phrase is "Vent lidt" (Wait a moment). It can also mean "to expect": "Hun venter barn" (She is expecting a baby).

sentence.da: Bussen er her ikke endnu, så vi må **vente**.
sentence.en: The bus is not here yet, so we have to wait.

at vente på.explanation: "At vente på" means "to wait for" someone or something. Danish says "på" (on) where English says "for": "Jeg venter på bussen" (I am waiting for the bus). "Vent!" means "Wait!".

sentence.da: Toget kommer ikke endnu, så jeg må **vente på** det.
sentence.en: The train is not coming yet, so I have to wait for it.

at vide.explanation: "At vide" means "to know" a fact: "Jeg ved det ikke" (I do not know). For knowing a person or a place, Danish uses a different word, "at kende" (to know someone).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **vide**, hvor du bor.
sentence.en: I would like to know where you live.

at ville.explanation: "At ville" means "to want to": "Jeg vil have en kop kaffe" (I want a cup of coffee). Adding "gerne" (gladly) makes it polite: "Jeg vil gerne have en kop kaffe" (I would like a cup of coffee). "Vil" is about wanting, not just "will", so for plans and duties use "skal" (have to, am going to).

sentence.da: Hun sagde, at hun **ville** have en kop te.
sentence.en: She said that she wanted a cup of tea.

at vinde.explanation: "At vinde" means "to win": "Vi vinder kampen" (We win the match). You can win a game, a prize or a race.

sentence.da: Vi kan **vinde** kampen, hvis vi spiller godt.
sentence.en: We can win the match if we play well.

at vise.explanation: "At vise" means "to show": "Jeg viser dig vej" (I show you the way). When you show someone something, the person comes first, with no word for "to" in front: "Hun viser mig bogen" (She shows me the book). "Vis mig" means "Show me". It is also used when a clock or a meter shows something.

sentence.da: Jeg kender ikke byen. Kan du **vise** mig vej?
sentence.en: I don't know the city. Can you show me the way?

at vågne.explanation: "At vågne" means "to wake up" by yourself: "Jeg vågner klokken syv" (I wake up at seven). When someone else wakes you, Danish uses "at vække" (to wake someone).

sentence.da: Jeg skal **vågne** klokken syv, så jeg sætter vækkeuret.
sentence.en: I have to wake up at seven, so I set the alarm clock.

at vågne op.explanation: "At vågne op" means "to wake up", the moment you become awake. People often just say "at vågne" (to wake up), so the "op" (up) is optional. Do not mix it up with "at stå op" (to get out of bed).

sentence.da: Telefonen ringer, og jeg må **vågne op**.
sentence.en: The phone rings, and I have to wake up.

at vælge.explanation: "At vælge" means "to choose" or "to pick": "Jeg vælger den røde" (I choose the red one). "Et valg" means both "a choice" and "an election".

sentence.da: Der er rød, blå og grøn. Du må **vælge** en.
sentence.en: There is red, blue and green. You may choose one.

at være.explanation: "At være" means "to be", and it is one of the most important words in Danish: "Jeg er træt" (I am tired). It is used for saying how someone is, where something is, and what someone is. The present form "er" is the same for everyone: "jeg er" (I am), "han er" (he is), "vi er" (we are).

sentence.da: Jeg er træt, så jeg vil **være** hjemme i dag.
sentence.en: I am tired, so I want to be at home today.

at være syg.explanation: "At være syg" means "to be sick" or "to be ill": "Jeg er syg" (I am sick). It covers anything from a cold to a serious illness. To get sick, say "at blive syg" (to become sick). To tell work you cannot come because you are sick, say "at melde sig syg" (to call in sick).

sentence.da: Jeg har feber og hoste, så jeg må **være syg** hjemme.
sentence.en: I have a fever and a cough, so I have to be sick at home.

at være væk.explanation: "At være væk" means "to be gone" or "to be away". It is used for people who are not there ("Han er væk", He is gone) and for things that have disappeared ("Min nøgle er væk", My key is gone). It describes being gone, not the act of leaving.

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke finde min nøgle. Den må **være væk**.
sentence.en: I can't find my key. It must be gone.

en vaccine.explanation: "En vaccine" means "a vaccine". It looks like the English word, but the stress is in the middle: vak-SEE-ne.

sentence.da: Lægen gav mig en **vaccine** mod influenza.
sentence.en: The doctor gave me a vaccine against the flu.

en vegetar.explanation: "En vegetar" means "a vegetarian", a person who does not eat meat. To say what you are, use "Jeg er vegetar" (I am a vegetarian). For food, use "vegetarisk", as in "en vegetarisk ret" (a vegetarian dish).

sentence.da: Jeg er **vegetar**, så jeg spiser ikke kød.
sentence.en: I am a vegetarian, so I do not eat meat.

en vej.explanation: "En vej" means "a road" and also "a way" or route: "Hvilken vej skal jeg gå?" means "Which way should I go?". "At spørge om vej" means "to ask for directions", with no "en" before "vej".

sentence.da: Vi gik langs en lang **vej** med mange træer.
sentence.en: We walked along a long road with many trees.

en vejrudsigt.explanation: "En vejrudsigt" means "a weather forecast", a description of what the weather will be like. It is made from "vejr" (weather) and "udsigt" (outlook).

sentence.da: Jeg læser en **vejrudsigt** på nettet, og i morgen regner det.
sentence.en: I read a weather forecast online, and tomorrow it will rain.

en ven.explanation: "En ven" means "a friend", usually a male friend, but it can be used for a friend of either sex. Be careful with "kæreste" (boyfriend or girlfriend): it means a romantic partner, not just a friend.

sentence.da: Min **ven** hjælper mig, når jeg er ked af det.
sentence.en: My friend helps me when I am sad.

en veninde.explanation: "En veninde" means "a female friend", used when the friend is a woman or girl. For a male friend, or a friend in general, use "en ven" (a friend).

sentence.da: Jeg ringer til min **veninde**, for hun er syg.
sentence.en: I am calling my (female) friend, because she is sick.

en verden.explanation: "En verden" means "a world". Common phrases are "i hele verden" (all over the world) and "verdens bedste" (the best in the world), where "verdens" means "the world's".

sentence.da: Hun rejser rundt i **verden**.
sentence.en: She travels around the world.

en vin.explanation: "En vin" means "a wine". You can name the colour: "en rødvin" (a red wine) or "en hvidvin" (a white wine). To order, say "et glas vin" (a glass of wine) or "en flaske vin" (a bottle of wine).

sentence.da: Vi bestiller en flaske **vin** til maden.
sentence.en: We order a bottle of wine for the meal.

en vinter.explanation: "En vinter" means "a winter". Use "om vinteren" for "in the winter" in general, and "i vinter" for "this winter".

sentence.da: En **vinter** i Danmark er kold og mørk.
sentence.en: A winter in Denmark is cold and dark.

en vinterjakke.explanation: "En vinterjakke" means "a winter jacket", a warm jacket. It is made from "vinter" (winter) and "jakke" (jacket).

sentence.da: Det er koldt i dag, så jeg tager min **vinterjakke** på.
sentence.en: It is cold today, so I put on my winter jacket.

en væg.explanation: "En væg" means "a wall" inside a building or room. For a wall outdoors, such as around a garden, Danes say "en mur" (a brick or stone wall).

sentence.da: Der hænger et billede på en **væg** i stuen.
sentence.en: A picture hangs on a wall in the living room.

et vandrerhjem.explanation: "Et vandrerhjem" means "a hostel", a cheap place to stay. It is built from "vandrer" (hiker) and "hjem" (home), so literally "a hiker's home".

sentence.da: Hotellet er dyrt, så vi bor på et **vandrerhjem**.
sentence.en: The hotel is expensive, so we stay at a hostel.

et venteværelse.explanation: "Et venteværelse" means "a waiting room", such as at the doctor or dentist. It is built from "vente" (to wait) and "værelse" (room). "Sid i venteværelset" means "Sit in the waiting room".

sentence.da: Vi sidder i et **venteværelse** og venter på lægen.
sentence.en: We sit in a waiting room and wait for the doctor.

et vindue.explanation: "Et vindue" means "a window". You can say "at åbne vinduet" (to open the window) or "at lukke vinduet" (to close the window).

sentence.da: Jeg åbner et **vindue**, fordi der er varmt.
sentence.en: I open a window because it is warm.

et visum.explanation: "Et visum" means "a visa", permission to enter or stay in a country. You apply for one with "at søge om" (to apply for): "Jeg søger om et visum" means "I am applying for a visa".

sentence.da: Før du rejser til landet, skal du søge om et **visum**.
sentence.en: Before you travel to the country, you must apply for a visa.

et værelse.explanation: "Et værelse" means "a room" in a home or hotel, a space for living or sleeping in. It is not "room" as in free space: for that Danes say "plads" (space, room). At a hotel you book "et værelse" for the night.

sentence.da: Jeg har booket et **værelse** til to nætter.
sentence.en: I have booked a room for two nights.

vand.explanation: "Vand" means "water". For water in general you use no "et" or "a": "Jeg drikker vand" (I drink water). To ask for a glass in a restaurant, say "Må jeg få et glas vand?" (May I have a glass of water?). "Koldt vand" means "cold water".

sentence.da: Må jeg bede om et glas **vand**?
sentence.en: May I have a glass of water?

varm.explanation: "Varm" means both "warm" and "hot", for weather, food, drinks and rooms: "varm kaffe" (hot coffee) and "en varm dag" (a warm day).

sentence.da: Suppen kommer lige fra komfuret, så den er meget **varm**.
sentence.en: The soup comes straight from the stove, so it is very hot.

varme.explanation: "En varme" means "heat" or "warmth". The same spelling also appears in "at varme" (to heat up) and "varme dage" (warm days), so the rest of the sentence tells you which one is meant.

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke tåle **varme**, så jeg bliver hjemme, når solen skinner.
sentence.en: I can't stand heat, so I stay at home when the sun is shining.

ved.explanation: "Ved" means "by" or "at" and shows that something is next to or near something: "ved vinduet" (by the window). Careful: "ved" is also the "I know" word in "Jeg ved det" (I know it). The rest of the sentence tells you which one is meant.

sentence.da: Han sidder **ved** vinduet.
sentence.en: He is sitting by the window.

ved siden af.explanation: "Ved siden af" means "next to" or "beside" and is used to say where things are: "Banken ligger ved siden af posthuset" (The bank is next to the post office). It can also mean "alongside", as in "ved siden af mit arbejde" (alongside my job).

sentence.da: Banken ligger **ved siden af** posthuset.
sentence.en: The bank is next to the post office.

vegetarisk.explanation: "Vegetarisk" means "vegetarian", meaning without meat, and describes food. In a restaurant you can ask "Har I noget vegetarisk?" (Do you have anything vegetarian?). For a person who is a vegetarian, say "en vegetar" (a vegetarian).

sentence.da: Jeg spiser ikke kød, så jeg vil gerne have en **vegetarisk** ret.
sentence.en: I don't eat meat, so I would like a vegetarian dish.

vejr.explanation: "Vejr" means "weather". You can ask "Hvordan er vejret?" (How is the weather?) and answer "Det er godt vejr" (It is good weather) or "Det er dårligt vejr" (It is bad weather).

sentence.da: Det er godt **vejr**, og solen skinner.
sentence.en: The weather is good and the sun is shining.

forms.en: Thanks for the meal. You're welcome.

velbekomme.explanation: "Velbekomme" means "enjoy your meal" when you serve food, and "you're welcome" when someone says "tak for mad" (thanks for the meal). It is only used about food and drink. For other thanks, say "selv tak" (you're welcome) or "det var så lidt" (it was nothing).

sentence.da: Her er suppen. **Velbekomme**!
sentence.en: Here is the soup. Enjoy!

velkommen.explanation: "Velkommen" means "welcome". Use it to greet guests, adding "til" (to) and the place: "velkommen til Danmark" (welcome to Denmark). Do not use it for "you're welcome", which is "selv tak" or "det var så lidt" (it was nothing).

sentence.da: **Velkommen** til vores hjem!
sentence.en: Welcome to our home!

venlig.explanation: "Venlig" means "friendly" or "kind", for people, voices and smiles. "Venlig hilsen" (kind regards) is how you end a letter or an email.

sentence.da: Hun er så **venlig**, og hun smiler altid til mig.
sentence.en: She is so friendly, and she always smiles at me.

venstre.explanation: "Venstre" means "left", as in the left side or the left hand. In directions you usually say "til venstre" (to the left).

sentence.da: Tag den første vej til **venstre**.
sentence.en: Take the first road on the left.

vent lidt.explanation: "Vent lidt" means "wait a bit" and is how you ask someone to hold on for a moment. "Lidt" means "a little", which softens the request, and adding "tak" (thanks) makes it politer.

sentence.da: **Vent lidt**, jeg finder min taske.
sentence.en: Wait a bit, I'm just finding my bag.

vest.explanation: "Vest" means "west". It is used in place names such as "Vestjylland" (western Jutland, the western part of the Danish mainland).

sentence.da: Solen går ned i **vest**.
sentence.en: The sun goes down in the west.

vi.explanation: "Vi" means "we". Use it when "we" are the ones doing something: "Vi bor her" (We live here). When "we" are on the receiving end, use "os" (us): "Han ser os" (He sees us).

sentence.da: Min mand og jeg bor i Aarhus. **Vi** har to børn.
sentence.en: My husband and I live in Aarhus. We have two children.

vi ses.explanation: "Vi ses" literally means "we see each other" and is the everyday way to say "see you" when parting. Add a time to be specific: "vi ses i morgen" (see you tomorrow) or "vi ses på fredag" (see you on Friday). In a more formal setting, use "på gensyn" (see you again).

sentence.da: Jeg skal gå nu. **Vi ses** i morgen!
sentence.en: I have to go now. See you tomorrow!

vi tales ved.explanation: "Vi tales ved" means "we'll talk" and is a friendly goodbye, mostly after a phone call or message, when you expect to speak again soon. Use "vi ses" (see you) instead when you expect to meet in person.

sentence.da: Jeg ringer i aften. **Vi tales ved!**
sentence.en: I'll call tonight. Talk soon!

vigtig.explanation: "Vigtig" means "important", for things, people, news and decisions: "en vigtig beslutning" (an important decision).

sentence.da: I morgen er en **vigtig** dag, så jeg går tidligt i seng.
sentence.en: Tomorrow is an important day, so I am going to bed early.

vind.explanation: "Vind" means "wind". To say it is windy, Danes use "at blæse" (to blow): "Det blæser" (It is windy).

sentence.da: Der er meget **vind** i dag, og min hat blæser af hovedet.
sentence.en: There is a lot of wind today and my hat is blowing off my head.

virkelig.explanation: "Virkelig" means "really" and adds strength: "virkelig god" (really good). On its own, "Virkelig?" (Really?) shows surprise or doubt.

sentence.da: Maden var **virkelig** god, jeg vil gerne have mere.
sentence.en: The food was really good, I would like some more.

vores.explanation: "Vores" means "our" or "ours". It never changes, whatever it describes: "vores hus" (our house), "vores bil" (our car), "vores venner" (our friends).

sentence.da: **Vores** hus ligger tæt på havnen.
sentence.en: Our house is close to the harbour.

vred.explanation: "Vred" means "angry". To say you are angry at someone, use "vred på" (angry at): "Jeg er vred på ham" (I am angry at him). It is fairly strong; for being a little annoyed Danes use "irriteret" (annoyed) or "sur" (grumpy).

sentence.da: Hun råber højt, fordi hun er **vred** på sin bror.
sentence.en: She shouts loudly because she is angry with her brother.

våd.explanation: "Våd" means "wet", for clothes, hair, the ground, or anything soaked with water: "Det regner, så jakken er våd" (It is raining, so the jacket is wet).

sentence.da: Hunden har været i søen, så den er helt **våd**.
sentence.en: The dog has been in the lake, so it is completely wet.

vågen.explanation: "Vågen" means "awake". "Er du vågen?" means "Are you awake?" The similar-looking "at vågne" means "to wake up": "Jeg vågnede klokken syv" (I woke up at seven).

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke sove, jeg er **vågen** hele natten.
sentence.en: I can't sleep, I am awake all night.

væk.explanation: "Væk" means "away" or "gone". It goes with words about moving or taking: "Hun løber væk" (She runs away) and "Tag den væk" (Take it away). "Min nøgle er væk" means "My key is gone". As an order, "Gå væk!" (Go away!) sounds rude.

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke finde min taske. Den er **væk**!
sentence.en: I can't find my bag. It is gone!

værre.explanation: "Værre" means "worse" and is the step up from "dårlig" (bad). Use it to compare: "Det er værre end før" (It is worse than before). In "et værre rod" (quite a mess) it adds emphasis.

sentence.da: I går var det dårligt vejr, men i dag er det endnu **værre**.
sentence.en: Yesterday the weather was bad, but today it is even worse.

forms.en: Here you go, here is your coffee.

værsgo.explanation: "Værsgo" is what you say when you hand someone something or invite them to go ahead. It covers "here you go", "please, help yourself" and "go ahead". The reply is usually "tak" (thanks). To answer a thank-you, say "selv tak" (you're welcome) instead.

sentence.da: **Værsgo**, her er din billet.
sentence.en: Here you go, here is your ticket.

værst.explanation: "Værst" means "worst" and is the step up from "værre" (worse), which comes from "dårlig" (bad): "Det er værst" (It is the worst).

sentence.da: Mandag var en dårlig dag, men tirsdag var **værst**.
sentence.en: Monday was a bad day, but Tuesday was the worst.
